claim: O-GlcNAcylation is the reversible post-translational addition of β-N-acetylglucosamine to serine and threonine residues of nuclear and cytoplasmic proteins.
source: O-GlcNAcylation is the reversible post-translational addition of β-N-acetylglucosamine to serine and threonine residues of nuclear and cytoplasmic proteins.
evidence: This is a well-established definition in the field, representing established scientific knowledge about O-GlcNAcylation.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation plays an important role in several cellular processes through the modification of thousands of protein substrates.
source: It plays an important role in several cellular processes through the modification of thousands of protein substrates.
evidence: This statement draws from established scientific consensus about the broad functional importance of O-GlcNAcylation.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation in humans is mediated by a single essential enzyme, O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT).
source: O-GlcNAcylation in humans is mediated by a single essential enzyme, O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field about the enzymatic basis of O-GlcNAcylation.

claim: OGT, together with the sole O-GlcNAcase OGA, form an intricate feedback loop to maintain O-GlcNAc homeostasis in response to changes in cellular O-GlcNAc using a dynamic mechanism involving nuclear retention of its fourth intron.
source: OGT, together with the sole O-GlcNAcase OGA, form an intricate feedback loop to maintain O-GlcNAc homeostasis in response to changes in cellular O-GlcNAc using a dynamic mechanism involving nuclear retention of its fourth intron.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field and likely references prior work on OGT regulation.

claim: SFSWAP is a trans-acting factor regulating OGT intron detention.
source: Using an O-GlcNAc responsive GFP reporter cell line, we identify SFSWAP, a poorly characterized splicing factor, as a trans-acting factor regulating OGT intron detention.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from the CRISPR screen and validation experiments.

claim: SFSWAP is a global regulator of retained intron splicing and exon skipping that primarily acts as a negative regulator of splicing.
source: We show that SFSWAP is a global regulator of retained intron splicing and exon skipping that primarily acts as a negative regulator of splicing.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RNA-seq data and alternate splicing analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Knockdown of SFSWAP leads to reduced inclusion of a 'decoy exon' present in the OGT retained intron.
source: In contrast, knockdown of SFSWAP leads to reduced inclusion of a 'decoy exon' present in the OGT retained intron which may mediate its role in OGT intron detention.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR and RNA-seq data showing changes in decoy exon inclusion upon SFSWAP knockdown.

claim: Global analysis of decoy exon inclusion in SFSWAP and UPF1 double knockdown cells indicate altered patterns of decoy exon usage.
source: Global analysis of decoy exon inclusion in SFSWAP and UPF1 double knockdown cells indicate altered patterns of decoy exon usage.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and alternate splicing analysis in double knockdown conditions.

claim: Intron retention refers to the lack of removal of specific introns in a transcript, resulting in full-length introns in an RNA.
source: Intron retention (IR) refers to the lack of removal of specific introns in a transcript, resulting in full-length introns in an RNA (Monteuuis et al., 2019; Rekosh and Hammarskjold, 2018).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: IR that leads to impaired cytoplasmic export and nuclear retention of the transcript is referred to as intron detention.
source: IR that leads to impaired cytoplasmic export and nuclear retention of the transcript is referred to as intron detention (Boutz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Detained introns are a common feature of mammalian transcriptomes.
source: Detained introns are a common feature of mammalian transcriptomes, but, unlike other forms of alternate splicing, intron detention controls the levels and timing of production of mature mRNA (Boutz et al., 2015; Braunschweig et al., 2014; Yap et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Intron detention controls the levels and timing of production of mature mRNA.
source: Detained introns are a common feature of mammalian transcriptomes, but, unlike other forms of alternate splicing, intron detention controls the levels and timing of production of mature mRNA (Boutz et al., 2015; Braunschweig et al., 2014; Yap et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: DI-containing transcripts may serve as nuclear reservoirs that are spliced in response to cellular environment.
source: DI-containing transcripts may serve as nuclear reservoirs that are spliced in response to cellular environment, or they may be transcriptional dead-ends that are subjected to nuclear degradation pathways (Boutz et al., 2015; Yap et al., 2012; Pendleton et al., 2018; Mauger et al., 2016; Ninomiya et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: DI-containing transcripts may be transcriptional dead-ends that are subjected to nuclear degradation pathways.
source: DI-containing transcripts may serve as nuclear reservoirs that are spliced in response to cellular environment, or they may be transcriptional dead-ends that are subjected to nuclear degradation pathways (Boutz et al., 2015; Yap et al., 2012; Pendleton et al., 2018; Mauger et al., 2016; Ninomiya et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The environmental cues that regulate intron detention of the human O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) transferase (OGT) protein have been defined.
source: The environmental cues that regulate intron detention of the human O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) transferase (OGT) protein have been defined, but the mechanisms of this regulation are not fully understood (Park et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The mechanisms of OGT intron detention regulation are not fully understood.
source: The environmental cues that regulate intron detention of the human O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) transferase (OGT) protein have been defined, but the mechanisms of this regulation are not fully understood (Park et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work and represents a knowledge gap.

claim: OGT encodes the sole enzyme responsible for the post-translational modification O-GlcNAc, where UDP-GlcNAc serves as the cofactor for addition of GlcNAc residues to the hydroxyl groups of serine and threonine residues of thousands of nuclear and cytoplasmic proteins.
source: OGT encodes the sole enzyme responsible for the post-translational modification O-GlcNAc, where UDP-GlcNAc serves as the cofactor for addition of GlcNAc residues to the hydroxyl groups of serine and threonine residues of thousands of nuclear and cytoplasmic proteins (Kreppel et al., 1997; Lubas et al., 1997; Bond and Hanover, 2015; Mannino and Hart, 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: OGA (O-GlcNAcase) is the sole enzyme responsible for removal of O-GlcNAc.
source: Conversely, OGA (O-GlcNAcase) is the sole enzyme responsible for removal of O-GlcNAc (Gao et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Cells maintain O-GlcNAc homeostasis by an intricate feedback mechanism involving intron detention of the OGT transcript.
source: Cells maintain O-GlcNAc homeostasis by an intricate feedback mechanism involving intron detention of the OGT transcript (Park et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Under conditions of high cellular O-GlcNAc (such as treatment with the OGA inhibitor thiamet G [TG]), intron 4 of OGT is detained, resulting in reduction in cytoplasmic OGT mRNA.
source: Under conditions of high cellular O-GlcNAc (such as treatment with the OGA inhibitor thiamet G [TG]), intron 4 of OGT is detained, resulting in reduction in cytoplasmic OGT mRNA.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge and prior work on OGT regulation.

claim: Under conditions of low cellular O-GlcNAc (such as glucose deprivation or treatment with the OGT inhibitor OSMI-1), the intron is rapidly excised, resulting in increased levels of cytoplasmic OGT mRNA.
source: However, under conditions of low cellular O-GlcNAc (such as glucose deprivation or treatment with the OGT inhibitor OSMI-1), the intron is rapidly excised, resulting in increased levels of cytoplasmic OGT mRNA.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge and prior work on OGT regulation.

claim: The OGA transcript is also regulated by intron detention, but with the inverse relationship to O-GlcNAc levels outcomes as OGT.
source: Interestingly, the OGA transcript is also regulated by intron detention, but with the inverse relationship to O-GlcNAc levels outcomes as OGT (Tan et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A cis-acting intronic splicing silencer (ISS) situated within OGT intron 4 is necessary for IR.
source: We previously identified a cis-acting intronic splicing silencer (ISS) situated within OGT intron 4 that is necessary for IR (Park et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The ISS overlaps with an ~150 bp unannotated 'decoy exon' possessing multiple weak 5′ and 3′ splice sites.
source: Subsequent work by other groups showed that the ISS overlaps with an ~150 bp unannotated 'decoy exon' possessing multiple weak 5′ and 3′ splice sites (Parra et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work by other groups.

claim: Deletion of the OGT decoy exon/ISS or even blocking of the decoy 5′ splice sites using morpholino oligonucleotides renders splicing of intron 4 constitutive.
source: Deletion of the OGT decoy exon/ISS or even blocking of the decoy 5′ splice sites using morpholino oligonucleotides renders splicing of intron 4 constitutive (Park et al., 2017; Parra et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: At least partial assembly of the spliceosome around the decoy is necessary for OGT intron detention even though splicing of the decoy exon does not occur.
source: This suggests the somewhat counterintuitive idea that at least partial assembly of the spliceosome around the decoy is necessary for OGT intron detention even though splicing of the decoy exon does not occur.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations cited.

claim: Decoy exons are present in many other retained intron containing genes, specifically those with longer retained introns.
source: Decoy exons are not unique to OGT and are present in many other retained intron containing genes, specifically those with longer retained introns (Parra et al., 2018; Pirnie et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The decoy exons mediate IR in these genes as well.
source: The decoy exons mediate IR in these genes as well, but the precise mechanism by which decoy exons regulate IR remains unclear.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge and citations.

claim: OGT has been proposed to be a 'master regulator' of detained intron splicing.
source: In addition to the role of OGT intron detention in buffering changes in cellular O-GlcNAc levels, OGT (and consequently O-GlcNAc) has been proposed to be a 'master regulator' of detained intron splicing (Tan et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Treatment of cells with the OGT inhibitor OSMI-2 for short time periods (~30 min) induces changes in OGT detention to buffer O-GlcNAc levels.
source: Treatment of cells with the OGT inhibitor OSMI-2 for short time periods (~30 min) induces changes in OGT detention to buffer O-GlcNAc levels.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge from prior work.

claim: Longer treatment durations (~2 hr) with OSMI-2 lead to global changes in detained intron splicing.
source: However, longer treatment durations (~2 hr) lead to global changes in detained intron splicing.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge from prior work.

claim: Differential phosphoproteomics after a short OSMI-2 treatment identified a set of proteins enriched in splicing factors.
source: Differential phosphoproteomics after a short OSMI-2 treatment identified a set of proteins enriched in splicing factors.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior work, likely from Tan et al., 2020.

claim: SFSWAP was identified as an 'early responder' in differential phosphoproteomics after OSMI-2 treatment.
source: These 'early responders' could potentially mediate downstream effects of OSMI-2 on splicing and included the putative splicing factor SFSWAP.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior work, likely from Tan et al., 2020.

claim: SFSWAP encodes the essential human homolog of the Drosophila splicing factor SWAP.
source: SFSWAP (splicing factor, suppressor of white-apricot homolog; SFRS8) encodes the essential human homolog of the Drosophila splicing factor SWAP (Denhez and Lafyatis, 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: SFSWAP is an alternate splicing factor containing an RS domain, but it does not possess a canonical RNA-binding domain.
source: It is an alternate splicing factor containing an RS domain, but it does not possess a canonical RNA-binding domain (Denhez and Lafyatis, 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: SFSWAP contains two suppressor of white apricot/Prp21 (SURP) domains which mediate its binding to other proteins containing an SURP interaction domain.
source: It contains two suppressor of white apricot/Prp21 (SURP) domains which mediate its binding to other proteins containing an SURP interaction domain.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about SFSWAP structure.

claim: The second SURP domain of SFSWAP has been shown to interact with the mammalian branchpoint binding protein SF1 in vitro.
source: The second SURP domain of SFSWAP has been shown to interact with the mammalian branchpoint binding protein SF1 in vitro (Crisci et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: SFSWAP regulates alternate splicing of Tau.
source: In addition, it regulates alternate splicing of Tau (Wang et al., 2004), CD45 and fibronectin (Sarkissian et al., 1996) by inhibiting the inclusion of specific exons.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: SFSWAP regulates alternate splicing of CD45 and fibronectin by inhibiting the inclusion of specific exons.
source: In addition, it regulates alternate splicing of Tau (Wang et al., 2004), CD45 and fibronectin (Sarkissian et al., 1996) by inhibiting the inclusion of specific exons.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Knockout of SFSWAP leads to enhanced splicing of the OGT detained intron, particularly under high-O-GlcNAc conditions.
source: We show that knockout of SFSWAP leads to enhanced splicing of the OGT detained intron, particularly under high-O-GlcNAc conditions, indicating its role as a negative regulator of OGT splicing.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: SFSWAP regulates OGT intron detention by modulating the inclusion or recognition of the decoy exon present within the detained intron.
source: Our results suggest that SFSWAP regulates OGT intron detention by modulating the inclusion or recognition of the decoy exon present within the detained intron.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data and inference from the results.

claim: SFSWAP may regulate decoy exon splicing globally to mediate its effect on intron detention.
source: Finally, global analysis of decoy exon splicing upon SFSWAP knockdown indicates that SFSWAP may regulate decoy exon splicing globally to mediate its effect on intron detention.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from global analysis.

claim: The GFP reporter construct reflects the response of endogenous OGT to intracellular O-GlcNAc levels.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that our GFP reporter construct reflects the response of endogenous OGT to intracellular O-GlcNAc levels.
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by experimental validation data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Treatment of reporter lines with 1 μM TG for 6 hr led to reduced levels of the spliced product.
source: Treatment of the reporter line with 1 μM TG for 6 hr led to reduced levels of the spliced product, while treatment with 10 μM OSMI-1 for the same time led to enhanced splicing increased levels of the reporter mRNA (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Treatment with 10 μM OSMI-1 for 6 hr led to enhanced splicing and increased levels of the reporter mRNA.
source: Treatment of the reporter line with 1 μM TG for 6 hr led to reduced levels of the spliced product, while treatment with 10 μM OSMI-1 for the same time led to enhanced splicing increased levels of the reporter mRNA (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: OGT was the top hit from the CRISPR screens.
source: As expected, the top hit from the screens was OGT itself (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by the MAGeCK analysis results shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The CRISPR screen identified many hits corresponding to genes involved in glucose metabolism including GFAT and SLC2A1.
source: In addition, we obtained many hits corresponding to genes involved in glucose metabolism including GFAT (Figure 1e) and SLC2A1 (a glucose transporter), further boosting our confidence that the genes identified in the screen are relevant to O-GlcNAc homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by the screen results shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The CRISPR screen obtained a few hits corresponding to RNA-binding proteins (e.g., HNRNPU, HuR) and proteins involved in m6A modification (ZC3H13, KIAA1429).
source: We also obtained a few hits corresponding to RNA-binding proteins (e.g., HNRNPU, HuR) and proteins involved in m6A modification (ZC3H13, KIAA1429).
evidence: This is supported by the screen results.

claim: The large majority of the hits from the CRISPR screen were splicing associated factors and/or components of the spliceosome.
source: Interestingly, the large majority of the hits were splicing associated factors and/or components of the spliceosome.
evidence: This is supported by the screen results shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Knockdown of SFSWAP increased GFP expression in the reporter line.
source: Consistently, knockdown of SFSWAP increased GFP expression (Figure 2b) and enhanced splicing of the reporter RNA (Figure 2c, left).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Knockdown of SFSWAP enhanced splicing of the reporter RNA.
source: Consistently, knockdown of SFSWAP increased GFP expression (Figure 2b) and enhanced splicing of the reporter RNA (Figure 2c, left).
evidence: This is supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Knockdown of SFSWAP in 293A-TOA cells under TG treatment conditions resulted in enhanced splicing of the retained intron compared to the non-target control.
source: Knockdown of SFSWAP in these cells under TG treatment conditions resulted in enhanced splicing of the retained intron compared to the non-target control (Figure 2c, right) indicating that the action of SFSWAP was not limited to the reporter.
evidence: This is supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Knockdown of SFSWAP resulted in a significant increase in the spliced form of OGT RNA compared to non-target both under DMSO (~1.8-fold) and TG-treated conditions (~3-fold).
source: Knockdown of SFSWAP resulted in a significant increase in the spliced form of OGT RNA compared to non-target both under DMSO (~1.8-fold) and TG-treated conditions (~3-fold).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The timing of enhanced intron 4 removal coincided with the timing of decrease in SFSWAP mRNA levels upon knockdown.
source: In addition, the timing of enhanced intron 4 removal coincided with the timing of decrease in SFSWAP mRNA levels upon knockdown, indicating a direct effect of SFSWAP knockdown on OGT intron 4 splicing (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by time-course data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Differential expression analysis revealed 252 downregulated and 633 upregulated genes on SFSWAP knockdown.
source: Differential expression analysis using edgeR (Supplementary file 3) revealed 252 downregulated and 633 upregulated genes on SFSWAP knockdown, but did not reveal any functional class of RNAs that was regulated by SFSWAP.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and differential expression analysis.

claim: The majority of alternate splicing changes between siNT and siSFSWAP occurred across retained introns and skipped exons.
source: Interestingly, we found global changes in splicing patterns between siNT and siSFSWAP, with the majority of changes occurring across two of the five event types analyzed – retained introns and skipped exons (Figure 3a, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by alternate splicing analysis using rMATS shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Knockdown of SFSWAP resulted in increased excision of retained introns globally.
source: Knockdown of SFSWAP resulted in increased excision of retained introns globally, indicated by more events with a positive value for IncLevelDiffference (Figure 3b) and as exemplified by genome browser shots of IFRD2 and GFUS/TSTA3 (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by alternate splicing analysis shown in Figure 3b and genome browser views in Figure 3c.

claim: SFSWAP autoregulates its own expression by control of splicing of its first two retained introns.
source: Previous observations that SFSWAP autoregulates its own expression by control of splicing of its first two retained introns is also consistent with this observation (Zachar et al., 1987; Zachar et al., 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In RIs that are more efficiently spliced upon SFSWAP knockdown, the average GC content in the RI and flanking exons was higher compared to those that less efficiently spliced.
source: In RIs that are more efficiently spliced upon SFSWAP knockdown (positive IncLevelDifference), we found that the average GC content in the RI and flanking exons was higher compared to those that less efficiently spliced (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 3d.

claim: In skipped exon events that result in enhanced inclusion upon SFSWAP knockdown, the skipped exon, upstream and downstream exons all had higher GC content.
source: We observed similar trends toward higher GC content when we examined skipped exon events that result in enhanced inclusion upon SFSWAP knockdown (negative IncLevelDifference). In this case, the skipped exon, upstream and downstream exons all had higher GC content.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 3d.

claim: There was reduced inclusion of the decoy exon upon SFSWAP knockdown under UPF1 knockdown conditions in the presence of TG.
source: Under these conditions, we saw reduced inclusion of the decoy exon upon SFSWAP knockdown (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: There was a ~5-fold reduction in sequencing reads containing the decoy exon upon SFSWAP knockdown.
source: Consistent with the RT-qPCR analysis, there was a ~5-fold reduction in sequencing reads containing the decoy exon upon SFSWAP knockdown (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by nanopore sequencing data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Decoy inclusion levels were significantly higher in either in UPF1 knockdown alone or TG treatment alone.
source: As a control, decoy inclusion levels were significantly higher in either in UPF1 knockdown alone (since the decoy exon form is stabilized) or TG treatment alone (Figure 4c, middle panels).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: RNA-seq analysis of SFSWAP knockdown cells in a UPF1 knockdown background detected a significant reduction in decoy usage.
source: Therefore, we performed RNA-seq analysis of SFSWAP knockdown cells (treated with TG) in a UPF1 knockdown background. Alternate splicing analysis using rMATS detected a significant reduction in decoy usage in SFSWAP knockdown cells in this background, consistent with the qPCR results (Figure 4c, right).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: SFSWAP promotes inclusion of the OGT decoy exon.
source: Thus, we conclude that SFSWAP promotes inclusion of the OGT decoy exon.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from RT-qPCR and RNA-seq.

claim: Decoy exon recognition is a critical component of regulation of OGT intron detention.
source: Because decoy exon recognition is a critical component of regulation of OGT intron detention, these data further suggest that SFSWAP regulates OGT intron detention by controlling decoy exon inclusion and/or recognition.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge from prior work.

claim: Decoy exons have been proposed to regulate IR in a large number of genes in addition to OGT, especially those with longer retained introns.
source: Decoy exons have been proposed to regulate IR in a large number of genes in addition to OGT, especially those with longer retained introns (Parra et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Decoy exons were either more or less included upon SFSWAP knockdown.
source: While the changes in retained intron splicing were primarily in the direction of increased splicing (i.e., less RI inclusion) and that of skipped exon splicing were predominantly in the direction of more inclusion upon SFSWAP knockdown, decoy exons were either more or less included (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by alternate splicing analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Decoy-containing retained intron events did not show a trend toward any direction upon SFSWAP knockdown.
source: In contrast to the enhanced removal of retained introns for most non-decoy exon-containing events upon SFSWAP knockdown (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 8), decoy-containing retained intron events did not show a trend toward any direction (Figure 5c), suggesting a different mechanism of regulation for decoy-containing retained introns.
evidence: This is supported by alternate splicing analysis shown in Figure 5c.

claim: There is a trend toward increased intron length for decoy-containing retained introns compared to non-decoy-containing retained introns.
source: Consistent with this observation and as observed by other groups (Boutz et al., 2015; Parra et al., 2018), we observed a trend toward increased intron length for decoy-containing retained introns compared to non-decoy-containing retained introns (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is supported by length distribution analysis shown in Figure 5d and citations to prior work.

claim: Mutation of the weak 5′ splice sites of the OGT decoy exon leads to constitutive splicing of exons 4 and 5 in reporters.
source: First, mutation of the weak 5′ splice sites of the OGT decoy exon leads to constitutive splicing of exons 4 and 5 in reporters.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior work on decoy exon function.

claim: eCLIP data demonstrate that U2AF1 and U2AF2 bind to the decoy 3′ splice sites.
source: Second, eCLIP data demonstrate that U2AF1 and U2AF2 bind to the decoy 3′ splice sites.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior work on decoy exon function.

claim: Addition of a morpholino antisense oligonucleotide targeting the OGT decoy's 5′ splice site promotes constitutive splicing of exons 4–5.
source: Third, addition of a morpholino antisense oligonucleotide targeting the OGT decoy's 5′ splice site also promotes constitutive splicing of exons 4–5.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior work on decoy exon function.

claim: Placing decoy exons and their flanking sequences into other heterologous introns leads to IR.
source: Fourth, placing decoy exons and their flanking sequences into other heterologous introns leads to IR, indicating that there is not a gene or intron-specific suppression of splicing.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior work on decoy exon function.

claim: CRISPR deletion of the endogenous locus containing the OGT decoy leads to constitutive splicing of exons 4 and 5.
source: Fifth, CRISPR deletion of the endogenous locus containing the OGT decoy leads to constitutive splicing of exons 4 and 5.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior work on decoy exon function.

claim: Only a small percentage of mature transcript spliced isoforms splice in the decoy, even when assayed in NMD-inhibiting condition.
source: Sixth, only a small percentage of mature transcript spliced isoforms splice in the decoy, even when assayed in NMD-inhibiting condition (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by nanopore sequencing data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Enrichment of known SRSF1-binding motifs was observed at the 5′ end of SFSWAP-dependent differentially regulated retained intron events and around differentially regulated exon skipping events.
source: Interestingly, we observed enrichment of known SRSF1-binding motifs at the 5′ end of SFSWAP-dependent differentially regulated retained intron events and around differentially regulated exon skipping events (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), supporting the idea that SRSF1 acts in concert with SFSWAP to mediate its effect.
evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: SF1 was identified as a potential target regulating OGT IR in the TG-treated CRISPR screen.
source: Notably, we also identified SF1 as a potential target regulating OGT IR in our TG-treated CRISPR screen (Figure 2) and could also validate SFSWAP-SF1 interactions in cell lines by co-immunoprecipitation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), further supporting this idea.
evidence: This is supported by CRISPR screen data shown in Figure 2.

claim: SFSWAP-SF1 interactions were validated in cell lines by co-immunoprecipitation.
source: Notably, we also identified SF1 as a potential target regulating OGT IR in our TG-treated CRISPR screen (Figure 2) and could also validate SFSWAP-SF1 interactions in cell lines by co-immunoprecipitation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), further supporting this idea.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: SFSWAP is one of the most highly differentially phosphorylated proteins in the cell after a short treatment (30 min) with an OGT inhibitor, OSMI-2.
source: This is supported by the observation that SFSWAP is one of the most highly differentially phosphorylated proteins in the cell after a short treatment (30 min) with an OGT inhibitor, OSMI-2 (Tan et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Treatment of cells with conditions leading to low O-GlcNAc levels lead to phosphorylation of SFSWAP at multiple residues (primarily S604).
source: Treatment of cells with conditions leading to low O-GlcNAc levels lead to phosphorylation of SFSWAP at multiple residues (primarily S604).
evidence: This statement is supported by prior work, likely from Tan et al., 2020.

claim: SFSWAP knockdown does not lead to complete excision of the OGT retained intron as is observed upon deletion of the decoy.
source: While we show that SFSWAP plays a major role in regulating OGT IR, we also realize that there are likely other factors at play in regulating OGT intron detention, especially given the fact that SFSWAP knockdown does not lead to complete excision of the OGT retained intron as is observed upon deletion of the decoy (Park et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an observation based on comparison of experimental data with prior work.

claim: The reporter consists of the entire intron 4 of OGT (the detained intron) and corresponding exons (exons 4 and 5) flanked upstream and downstream by the efficiently spliced β-globin intron 2 (and corresponding exons 2 and 3).
source: The reporter consists of the entire intron 4 of OGT (the detained intron) and corresponding exons (exons 4 and 5) flanked upstream and downstream by the efficiently spliced β-globin intron 2 (and corresponding exons 2 and 3) (Figure 1a; Scarborough et al., 2022).
evidence: This describes the reporter construct design shown in Figure 1a.

claim: An eGFP reporter upstream of this assembly is driven by a constitutive CMV promoter and translationally separated from the remaining exons by a T2A element.
source: An eGFP reporter upstream of this assembly is driven by a constitutive CMV promoter and translationally separated from the remaining exons by a T2A element (Donnelly et al., 2001a).
evidence: This describes the reporter construct design with citation to prior work on T2A.

claim: The T2A element induces ribosomal skipping producing a GFP polypeptide separate from the protein product of the β-globin-OGT exons.
source: The T2A element induces ribosomal skipping (Donnelly et al., 2001b) producing a GFP polypeptide separate from the protein product of the β-globin-OGT exons.
evidence: This describes the function of T2A with citation to prior work.

claim: Treatment of cells with the OGA inhibitor TG induces high O-GlcNAc levels.
source: Treatment of cells with the OGA inhibitor TG induces high O-GlcNAc levels.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the effect of TG treatment.

claim: Treatment with OGT inhibitor OSMI-1 induces a low O-GlcNAc condition.
source: On the other hand, treatment with OGT inhibitor OSMI-1 induces a low O-GlcNAc condition, which should promote intron 4 splicing, cytoplasmic export of the mRNA, and increased GFP expression (Figure 1a, right).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the effect of OSMI-1 treatment.

claim: RT-PCR analysis of reporter RNA from clonal cell lines yielded a predominant single band corresponding to the mature reporter mRNA indicating the absence of unexpected splicing events.
source: RT-PCR analysis of reporter RNA from clonal cell lines yielded a predominant single band corresponding to the mature reporter mRNA indicating the absence of unexpected splicing events (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The reporter mRNA band increased upon OSMI-1 treatment and decreased upon TG treatment.
source: Moreover, this band increased and decreased upon OSMI-1 and TG treatment, as expected.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Treatment of the reporter cells with glucosamine or the OGA inhibitor PUGNAc resulted in reduced GFP protein levels similar to TG.
source: Treatment of the reporter cells with glucosamine or the OGA inhibitor PUGNAc (O-(2-Acetamido-2-deoxy-D-glucopyranosylidene)amino N-phenyl carbamate) resulted in reduced GFP protein levels similar to TG, while treatment with the GFAT inhibitor DON (6-diazo-5-oxo-L-norleucine) or glucose deprivation led to increased GFP levels (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Treatment with the GFAT inhibitor DON or glucose deprivation led to increased GFP levels.
source: Treatment of the reporter cells with glucosamine or the OGA inhibitor PUGNAc (O-(2-Acetamido-2-deoxy-D-glucopyranosylidene)amino N-phenyl carbamate) resulted in reduced GFP protein levels similar to TG, while treatment with the GFAT inhibitor DON (6-diazo-5-oxo-L-norleucine) or glucose deprivation led to increased GFP levels (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Knockdown of OGT resulted in increased levels of reporter mRNA.
source: As expected, we observed increased levels of reporter mRNA upon OGT knockdown (Figure 1f), and this effect masked the effect of subsequent inhibitor treatments.
evidence: This is supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Pilot screens were performed at 100× library coverage with a 10-day knockout time period and 24-hr treatment with inhibitors just before selection.
source: We performed pilot screens at 100× library coverage with a 10-day knockout time period and 24-hr treatment with inhibitors just before selection for either 'high' or 'low GFP' cells by FACS sorting.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the CRISPR screen.

claim: Two additional replicates of the screen were performed at 300× coverage under TG treatment conditions only.
source: Since the list of putative targets from both screens were comparable (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2), we performed two additional replicates of the screen at 300× coverage under TG treatment conditions only and obtained similar results.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the replicate CRISPR screens.
